articleTitle: Submillimeter Model Measurements and their Applications to Millimeter Radar Systems
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A submillimeter-based modeling system has been developed and employed to obtain imaging and radar cross section (RCS) measurements of scale model targets. In these demonstration experiments three submillimeter frequencies at 1288, 2542, and 3125 GHz, obtained from a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> optically pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH laser were used to model 37, 70, and 90 GHz, respectively. In addition, a CD<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH laser line at 37.6 μm (7980 GHz) has been used to extend these measurements up to 228 GHz. The results obtained demonstrate that the system is capable of providing quantitative radar data.

articleTitle: Subharmonically-Pumped Millimeter-Wave Receivers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Subharmonically-pumped Schottky-barrier diode receivers with single-sideband receiver noise temperatures of 2500-3000 K from 200-230 GHz have been developed. The receivers have an instantaneous bandwidth exceeding 500 MHz and require about 10 dBm of local oscillator power at 100-115 GHz.

articleTitle: Integrated Monolithic Mixers on GaAs for Millimeter and Submillimeter Wave Applications
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The development of surface-oriented Schottky diodes for use as detectors and mixers has provided the potential for reliable low-cost monolithic receivers and the possibility of receiver arrays for the microwave, millimeter and submillimeter wave regions. Applications range from radio astronomy, plasma diagnostics and spectroscopy to large military imaging systems. Improved materials growth, ion-implantation and proton-bombardment-isolation technologies which have made the present surface-oriented devices possible are discussed. Integrated monolithic receivers in which antennas, transmission lines, and other circuit components are integrated with surface-oriented devices on a GaAs wafer are described.

articleTitle: Infrared Spectroscopy using a Photoacoustic Cell
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Photoacoustic spectroscopy is a technique useful for the study of solid and liquid samples when the samples are difficult to analyze by conventional infrared techniques, such as compressed KBr pellets, diffuse reflectance and attenuated total reflectance. A photoacoustic cell designed by Blank and Wakefield [1] and shown in Figure 1 is described. The magnitude of the signal in the photoacoustic cell is proportional to the amount of photon flux emanating from the sample. Therefore, a close correspondence exists between the strength of the acoustic signal and the amount of light absorbed by the sample. The photoacoustic cell has been used as an accessory with both a constant and variable mirror scan Michelson interferometer.

articleTitle: Efficient, High-Power D2O Laser Oscillator at 385 μm
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We have developed a high-power, narrow linewidth D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O vapor laser oscillator at 385 μm optically pumped by the 9R(22) CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser transition for Thomson scattering plasma diagnostics. The submillimeter (SMM) laser requirements for Thomson scattering are a megawatt power level in a pulse length of 150 to 200 ns with a linewidth less than 100 MHz FW at 0.1 maximum [1]. Previous oscillator-amplifier combinations [2] have failed to satisfy the narrow-linewidth requirement because of broad band superradiance from the amplifier. Therefore, we have concentrated our efforts on the development of an efficient high-power oscillator. Our early SMM oscillator designs incorporating a high finesse Fox-Smith mode selector [2] had the required linewidth but were very inefficient in converting CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser pump energy to SMM laser energy (∼ 0.04%). Since then work has been done to identify the 385 μm D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O laser as a stimulated Raman laser [3,4] and we have shown the importance of single mode and frequency tunable CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser pumping [4,5]. This previous work in combination with SMM oscillator design refinements presented in this report have allowed us to improve the SMM oscillator energy conversion efficiency by over a factor of six (0.26%) at a peak SMM output energy of 90 mJ in pulse lengths between 100 and 150 ns.

articleTitle: Michelson Output Coupler with 1-Dimensional Grid for an Optically Pumped near Millimeter Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The characteristics of a cw optically pumped near millimeter laser using Michelson output coupling and a wire-grid beamsplitter are described. The output polarization is found to be uniquely determined regardless of slight misalignment, in contrast to results obtained with a two-dimensional mesh.

articleTitle: IR-FIR Stark Spectroscopy of CH3OH Around the 9-P(34) CO2 Laser Line
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The assignment of the FIR lines from CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH is difficult as a consequence of the internal rotation and the asymmetry of the molecule. The rotational levels are labelled by the four quantum numbers (J, n, τ, K), where n and τ are related to the three-fold internal rotation potential. With the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> 9-P(34) pump two strong emissions at 70.5 μm and 40.2 μm were reported, together with weaker lines. The assignment of all these lines was proposed in [1] on the basis of wavelengths and relative polarizations measurements, and confirmed by our group investigation on the Stark effect of the FIR output at 70.5 μm [2,3]. Stark laser emission at 70.5 μm was detected for electric fields up to about 1.4 KV/cm. By a proper tuning of the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> pump frequency new strong CW FIR laser emission could be observed at 208 ± 2 μm and 205 ± l μm, for electric fields higher than 900 V/cm and 1050 V/cm respectively (E ⊥ to pump polarization). These emissions are originated from absorbing transitions which at zero electric field are close to but not in resonance with the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> 9P-(34) line. Informations on the rotovibrational spectroscopy of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH can be inferred by Stark effect investigation on the new FIR emissions, directly, and on the IR related pumps, through the transferred Lamb-dip technique (TLD) [4].

articleTitle: Coupling Optimization of Point Contact Detectors and Mixers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: One shows that, for a given IR power, the angular width of an illuminating focused laser beam can be adjusted to optimize the electromagnetic coupling. The predicted conditions have been checked experimentally for various devices (Schottky, MIM, Josephson) at 337, 70 and 10.6 μm.

articleTitle: Near-Millimeter Wave Radiometric Imaging
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A unique feature of the far infrared/near millimeter wave spectral region is that many dielectric and organic media that are opaque in the visible and infrared become transparent [1-4]. Thus it is possible to image these materials or “see through” them for the purpose of inspection, non-destructive testing or concealed object detection. The resolution is degraded relative to the visible and infrared imagery, however, it is still adequate for many applications. To demonstrate the potential of far infrared/near millimeter wave imagery, a simple imaging apparatus was constructed in our laboratory several years ago [3, 4]. Small samples, placed on a mechanical stage negotiating a raster scan, were interposed between an FIR laser and a liquid helium cooled GaAs detector. The amplified detector output modulated a light emitting diode affixed to the stage, and the photographic recording of the diode signal provided an optical rendition of the far infrared transmission (or reflection) image of the object. While this early system demonstrated many of the useful features of FIR/NMMW imagery, the restrictions of active illumination and helium cooled detection, and the ability to examine only small objects limited the utility of the approach.

articleTitle: Formulation of Non-Linear Free Electron Laser Dynamics with Space Charge Effects and Spatially Varying Wiggler
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The recent development of a class of lasers in which the active medium is a relativistic stream of electrons has the exciting possibility of becoming a new source of coherent, high power, continuously tunable radiation [1,2]. Furthermore, recent theoretical studies [3-8] have shown that efficiencies of the order of 20% and higher can be realized at optical frequencies. The free electron laser (FEL) is characterized by a pump field, for example a spatially periodic magnetic field, which scatters off a relativistic electron beam. In this paper we present a brief outline of the formulation of the non-linear equations which describes the FEL mechanism. These equations are written in normalized form and are applicable to both the low and high gain regimes of the FEL. They also include space charge effects and apply to variable period magnetic pump fields (wigglers).

articleTitle: Submm Stark Spectroscopy of Methanol
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A systematic investigation of the Stark effect on the optically pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH FIR laser lines is carried on in our laboratory. CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH was selected among many other molecules because i) it has the largest number of laser lines, ranging from 37.5 μm up to the mm region, ii) many of these lines are very strong.iii) CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH has a complex spectrum, and a new approach with complementary information will be a valuable help in order to get a deeper insight.

articleTitle: Quasi-Imaging near Millimeter Radar
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Visible light and FLIR imaging systems provide detailed imagery suitable for acquisition and recognition of tactical targets at ranges up to several kilometers, as long as suitable propagation conditions exist. However, when visibility is limited by fogs or battlefield smokes, such systems are blinded and other means must be provided. A Near Millimeter Wave (NMMW) quasi-imaging system shows promise in satisfying this critical requirement [1, 2]. Propagation of near millimeter waves through the clear air (where water vapor is the principal cause of attenuation), and through fogs and smokes, improves with increasing wavelength [3]. But resolution, and therefore imaging performance, improves with decreasing wavelength. The tradeoff between propagation and resolution dominates other system design characteristics.

articleTitle: High Resolution Spectroscopy of Some Gaseous Molecules with an Infrared Fourier Interferometer
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A Michelson type Fourier interferometer having a maximum resolution of 0.06 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> between 5 and 20000 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> (2000-0.5 μm) is described. Fig. 1 shows the optical diagram of the interferometer. The spectrometer is interfaced to a data system that can be expandable to 80K of memory. Measurements on some gaseous molecules made with the spectrometer are shown and discussed. As examples of the instrument's performance, Figs. 2 and 3 show respectively the high resolution spectra of nitrous oxide [1] in the submillimeter region and the spectrum of the atmospheric oxygen band in the visible region at about 760 nm.

articleTitle: Photon Drag Detection
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Although photon drag was first observed ten years ago [1] [2] detectors utilizing this effect have been largely confined to CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser wavelengths. Commercially available detectors are calibrated for 10.6 μm and although they can be used at other wavelengths various pitfalls can arise. Figure 1 shows the voltage responsivity of a typical p-type germanium detector between 2.5 and 13 μm. It is disconcerting to find that not only does the responsivity vary rapidly with wavelength, but the sign of the signal changes five times.

articleTitle: Atmospheric Turbulence Effects on Infrared and Near-Millimeter Wave Propagation [1]
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Scintillation of electromagnetic energy traversing the turbulent atmosphere is caused by refractive index inhomogeneities in the path that cause phase shifts, giving rise to selective reinforcement or degradation of the energy across the beam. The resulting energy distribution is log normal [2], characterized by a variance s<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">E</inf><sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> that is a function of the degree of atmospheric turbulence. These inhomogeneities also cause angle of arrival fluctuations, depolarization, frequency shift, and thermal blooming; although the latter three effects are thought to be of minor importance in the NMMW spatial region.

articleTitle: Molecular Parameters Determining the Performance of CW Optically Pumped FIR Lasers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In the past, a set of selection criteria based on key molecular properties were used to successfully predict the discovery of the optically pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>F<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser [1]. About fifty lines have now been discovered with this molecule [2] which has several strong lines with conversion efficiencies greater than 30% of the theoretical limit [3], Wide variation in the performance of the various lines of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>F<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> has been observed and could only be analyzed with line assignments for the laser transitions. Many of the strong lines have been assigned by analogy with the CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>OH molecule which has similar types of FIR laser transitions.

articleTitle: Experiments for Sensitivity Enhancement of a Heterodyne Detection System at Submm Wavelength
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Recently the heterodyning technique has been extended into the submm range using quasi optical coupling structures. The coupling losses of the typically 4λ long wire antenna were reduced by combining it with a corner reflector erected parallel to the wire axis [1, 2, 3]. With an optically pumped submm laser as local oscillator a conversion loss L<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">O</inf> = 17.5 dB (SSB) has been achieved [4].

articleTitle: Millimeter/Submillimeter Nonlinear Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The techniques of coherent transient spectroscopy have been successfully applied to the microwave and optical regions but lack of suitable sources has prevented extension to the millimeter/submillimeter wavelength region where several strong molecular transitions occur. This paper analyzes the experimental requirements and theory for such experiments considering several molecules including CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Cl and H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O.

articleTitle: Saturated and Small Signal Gain in CW Laser-Pumped FIR Laser Gases
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The gain process in the gases for the FIR Laser can be completely described by the quantum mechanical theory of the three-level system. This paper reports the saturated and the small signal gains of the 7 0 μm and the 119 μm transitions in CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH, obtained by solving the density matrix equations for a three-level system /1/ for arbitrary pump- and FIR fields. The results are valid for arbitrary broadenings (Doppler/pressure) of the transitions involved, and also account for the removed M-degeneracy of the molecular levels due to the linearly polarized laser fields.

articleTitle: Projected Reduction of Submillimeter Wave Mixer Noise at 77 K by the use of InSb Schottky Barrier Diodes
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Because of its low effective mass, InSb exhibits a high electron mobility. Since a high conductivity would reduce the parasitic losses, this material has been proposed for Schottky-barrier mixer diodes in the submillimeter region. Progress in ultra-high-vacuum deposition techniques makes the construction of a rectifying barrier on N-type InSb now appear feasible. However, the expenditure that will be required to solve the interface problem makes a serious evaluation of the benefits of InSb over GaAs necessary.

articleTitle: Optical Material Literature Index for the Near-Millimeter Wave Spectral Region
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The primary frequency interval of interest here is the near-millimeter wave spectral region (NMMW—roughly 0.3 to 3 mm). This spectral region falls between the more actively researched far infrared and millimeter regions but has not itself received much attention until recently. Work has gone on at a relatively low level of effort, conducted by diverse microwave and infrared groups, using many different techniques, reporting in various wavelength and parameter notations in diverse journals. This paper reports on the preparation of a literature index to these references, and on observations based on that index. Particular thanks is due to Birch and Parker for their extensive bibliography on dispersive Fourier transform spectrometry [1], from which a number of material references were obtained. The emphasis in the index prepared thus far is on solid materials. Over 400 entries are included, taken from over 100 references. The format of the index is an alphabetical listing of materials, mostly by chemical name with cross referencing for more common names.

articleTitle: Far Infrared Laser Thermal Spectroscopy of Superconductors
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: An optically pumped far infrared laser provides fixed photon energies near the superconducting gap, making it possible to carry out experiments where the temperature is swept through T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">C</inf>. Such thermal measurements in thin films of V<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Si show both known and unexplained features, with some of the latter perhaps due to a second gap.

articleTitle: Precise Pump and Emission Wavelengths for New CH OH Laser Lines
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The importance of methyl alcohol in submillimeter (SMM) laser research is well know. It was one of the first molecules to be used for SMM generation via optical pumping with a CW CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser [1], and has been one of the most fertile up to now, generating radiation in the wavelength ∼ 40μm to ∼ 1200μm [2]. Some of the basic reasons for its success are the excellent overlap between the C-O strech mode and the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser spectrum. The complexity of the torsional-rotational spectrum, the liberal selection rules caused by the asymmetry of the molecule and the large dipole moments associated with as well the internal as the overall rotation. Therefore, good spectroscopic data for CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH, particularly on the rotational structure of excited vibrational states, is essential for better understanding the laser emission. Inversely, assignments of the SMM laser emission can serve as a basis for modeling this molecule. Work in this direction has been published lately [3-5], but the experimental basis has still to be expanded to gain a clear understanding of the vibrationally excited CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH molecule. For this purpose, the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-TEA laser seems a suitable pumping source: the possibility of off-resonance pumping and its broad linewidth which increases the chances of coincidences with molecular absorption lines should lead to many new SMM laser emissions. However, initial results [6-7] have been disappointing since only 3 new SMM lines were discovered but better spectral matching between the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-TEA laser and the CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH absorption line [8] improved these performances. We now report the measurements of many new SMM laser lines in CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH via optical pumping by a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-TEA laser. Some of these originate from pump transitions for which SMM emission has not previously been observed.

articleTitle: The Theory of Electron Cyclotron Maser Devices
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The electron cyclotron maser (gyrotron) is an extremely promising device for efficiently generating coherent, high-power millimeter and sub-millimeter radiation. This paper describes the physical mechanism of the maser as well as the recent theoretical progress made in dramatically a) enhancing the maser efficiency by contouring the external magnetic field and b) increasing the operating bandwidth in the slow wave maser amplifier by employing a dielectrically loaded waveguide.

articleTitle: Stimulated Electron Radiation in a Medium due to Wiggled Magnetic Field
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The PDECC (partial differential equations respect to coupling constants) formalism [1,2] is used to derive the S matrix suitable for treating the stimulated radiation when an electron interacts with a static wiggled magnetic field in a dielectric medium. articleTitle: Very Short Far Infrared Pulses from Optically Pumped CH3OH/D, Chooh and CH3F Lasers using an Eq-Switched CO2 Laser as a Pump Source
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: This paper describes the generation of far infrared pulses with a risetime of 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−8</sup>s from optically pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH/D, CHOOH and CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F lasers using a Q-switched current pulsed CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser as a pump source. The pump source consists of a conventional tunable low pressure (20 Torr) CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser which is Q-switched by a rotating mirror mounted on an air-driven spindle. Discharge current pulses up to 200 mA and 100-300 μs duration are produced and synchronized to the Q-switch by a trigger pulse from the rotating mirror. Due to the high discharge current, output powers are increased by at least a factor 5 with respect to Q-switched pulses from a d.c. current mode (20 mA). This leads to kW peak power pulses even at transitions such as 9P38, 9P6 and 9R6 which are especially important for pumping CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH and CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OD. The pump pulses are focussed by an f = 50 cm mirror onto the 1 mm incoupling hole of the FIR cavity, which consists of a 1 m long 13 mm diameter quartz tube and two 25 mm diameter flat mirrors.

articleTitle: Generation of Ultrashort Pulses in Synchronous Pumping of Near-Millimeter Wave Lasers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The generation of high power, ultrashort (τ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">p</inf> << 1 nsec) near-millimeter wave pulses of radiation is of significant interest in many potential applications. In the optically pumped molecular gases, which form an important class of FIR/NMM coherent sources, there are further questions about the ability of these generally narrow band systems to support wideband pulse amplification and oscillations. We have experimentally examined the character of NMM wave emission in selected gases when optically pumped with pulsed excitation in an arrangement which synchronously matches pump laser and NMM wave cavities. Under optimal conditions we observe high power NMM wave emission in bursts which are significantly shorter than the approximately nanosecond pump laser excitation.

articleTitle: Submillimetre Absorption of Electrolyte Solutions
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: This work is a part of a research plan of the GR4/CNRS, concerning the study of ion-ion and ion-solvent interactions in electrolyte solutions. In a first step, information have been obtained by dielectric relaxation and conductivity measurements about (i) the ionic association (ii) the perturbation of Debye rotation by ionic solvation [1]. Now, our purpose is to undertake investigations about the absorption processes in such materials which occur at times shorter than 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−12</sup>s corresponding to the submillimeter wavelength range. Previous works have already shown the interest of the far infrared (FIR) spectroscopy applied to electrolyte solutions, essentially in two directions. At first, for tetraalkylammonium halides solutions in non polar solvents, a strong absorption has been shown to arise from interionic vibrations providing a possible way to test ionic pair potential models [2]. Secondly, numerous investigations have been made about the strong absorption band ascribed to solvated cations. This band due to the short range cation-solvent interactions peaks around 400 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> for Li<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">+</sup> and at wavenumbers lower or equal to 200 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> for the other alkaline cations. In this paper, we present power absorption coefficient data a at wavenumbers lower than 320 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> for lithium salts solutions in various polar solvents : tetrahydrofuran (THF), 1,3-dioxolan, 1,2-dimethoxyethane. Lithium salts solutions have been chosen in order to avoid an undesirable overlap with the solvated cation band. Such spectral measurements are very difficult with the usual FIR low power sources because these liquids are very absorbing. All polar solvents exhibit a broad, strong absorption band generally ascribed to the libration of dipoles in the cage constituted by the surrounding molecules. Its maximum is situated in the 30-100 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> region. Another difficulty is we need to compare the solvent and solution spectra in order to evidence the effects of the solute. In these conditions, we have decided to combine the use of a conventional Fourier transform interferometer and a FIR spectrometer to cover the range 20-320 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup>.

articleTitle: Photon Drag and Radiation Pressure in Refractive Media
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The correct expression for momentum density and hence pressure of radiation in a medium of refractive index n has been an open question for half a century. According to Minkowski[1], it depends on DxB and the momentum of a photon should be nhv/c, whereas Abraham[2] favours an ExH dependence leading to photon momentum hv/nc.

articleTitle: Anomalous Absorption in Fluctuating Valence Compounds
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We have shown for the first time that fluctuating valence compounds have a characteristic broad absorption maximum in the far infrared. The absorptivity peak near 150 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> in CePd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>, absent in the isostructural compound YPd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>, arises from fluctuations of the cerium ion valence between the 3+ and 4+ state.

articleTitle: Design of a Far Infrared Interferometer for the Large European Tokamak (Jet)
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The design of the JET interferometer is extrapolated from the multichannel apparatus operated on TFR since several years [1].

articleTitle: A Double Pass Rapid Scanning Fourier Transform Spectrometer for Plasma Diagnostics
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In recent years measurements of the spectrum of electron cyclotron emission from high-temperature tokamak plasmas is becoming increasingly important for the diagnostic of the electron temperature [1-4]. The authors have developed a rapid scanning Fourier transform spectrometer (FTS) system to measure the radiation from JIPP T-II tokamak device [5]. The JIPP T-II has a major radius of 91 cm and a plasma radius of 15 cm, in which the free electrons are confined with toroidal field up to 3 T. These electrons gyrate at the electron cyclotron frequency w<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">ce</inf> = eB/m and emit radiation at frequencies w = n w<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">ce</inf> (n = 1, 2, 3 …) which is called electron cyclotron radiation. The radiation are broadened by an known inhomogeneity in the magnetic field. By measuring the spectrum of the cyclotron radiation, the informations on the electron temperature of the plasma are obtained. The specific intensity of emitted radiation I [W/m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> sterad, Hz] is given by Kirchoff's radiation law as, I = (w<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/8 Π<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) kTe [1 - exp(-τ)], where w is the frequency of the radiation, kTe the electron energy, τ the optical depth of the medium and c the speed of light. The black body intensity is I<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">b</inf> = (w<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>/8 Π<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) kTe at high temperature and long wavelength, where Rayleigh-Jeans approximation is valid. When the optical depth of the plasma is greater than about 2, the plasma radiates and absorbs as a black body and the electron temperature as a function of radius is obtained simply by measuring the power emitted by the plasma as a function of frequency. In JIPP T-II, for the extraordinary mode, the second harmonic is optically thick (τ ∼ 30), and the first and the third are optically thin. Therefore, it is reasonable to pick up the second harmonic out of them. The full bandwidth of the second harmonic is estimated to be 51.2 GHz. To represent the profile correctly, several points are needed at least. So that, the resolution higher than 8 GHz is demanded. We devised a FTS which satisfies the requirement. It is presented in the following.

articleTitle: A Scintillation Theory for Millimetre and Submillimetre Wavebands
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Scintillation is the observed fluctuation in intensity and apparent position of sources of small angular size and is caused by random fluctuations in the refractive index of the earth's atmosphere through which the signals propagate. In the visible waveband the refractive index variations are associated with the fluctuation of the temperature of the atmosphere due to turbulence [2]. At longer radio wavelengths the variation of the electron density in the ionosphere is the cause of radio scintillations. At shorter radio wavelengths, where the ionosphere exerts a diminishing influence, variations in the water vapour concentration of the troposphere become of increasing importance [3]. In all of these regions the medium is essentially non-absorbing and attenuation of the signal in the turbulent region plays an insignificant role. For the millimetre and submillimetre wavebands, however, this is no longer the case. The purpose of the theory to be presented is not just to allow for attenuation but to deduce from the fluctuations in atmospheric attenuation, the amount of scintillation present and to predict the atmospheric limit to resolution.

articleTitle: RIB Waveguide for Submillimeter-Wave Circuits
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: It is anticipated that dielectric waveguides will be used as the fundamental transmission line for integrated millimeter and submillimeter wave circuits. A dielectric rib waveguide will become one of the most important waveguides. This paper deals with its transmission properties. The analytical consideration is performed by considering the boundary conditions in the least-squares sense. Many experiments, together with our analysis prove the usefulness of this guide in the millimeter and submillimeter-wave regions.

articleTitle: Al + O2 Superconducting Bolometer
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Bolometers are known to be efficient detectors covering microwaves to far infrared with a relative constant sensibility. We need, in our laboratory, a bolometer with the highest response covering this range, a short time constant being not necessary.

articleTitle: Magnetoplasma-Reflectivity of Pb1-XGeXTe
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Pb<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1-X</inf>Ge<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">X</inf>Te exhibits a structural phase transition from the cubic NaCl(O<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">h</inf>) to the rhombohedral As-like structure (C<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3v</inf>) at low lattice temperatures [1]. The transition temperature T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">C</inf> is a steep function of the Ge content. The infrared active mode of the cubic structure is split into an A<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf>-mode and a double degenerate E-mode. These modes are both infrared and Raman active. A<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf> is observable for the polarization <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">→</sup>E‖ c-axis [2,3]. In the cubic phase, electrons or holes are located in four equivalent L-valleys. Below T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">C</inf>, there are three equivalent L-valleys, and along the direction of the c-axis a T-valley.

articleTitle: Low Noise 86–88 GHz Traveling Wave Maser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We describe the fabrication and performance of a traveling wave maser using iron doped rutile (Fe<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3+</sup>:TiO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) for a signal frequency of 86-88 GHz. The electronic gain is 36 dB with a 3 dB bandwidth of 40-50 MHz and a net maser gain of 15-20 dB. The maser input noise temperature has been measured as T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">Maser</inf> = 20 ± 10 K.

articleTitle: FIR Scattering Measurements from Laboratory Plasmas
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The application of the far infrared (FIR) region of the spectrum to plasma diagnostics has already provided significant improvements over existing systems in areas such as interferometric and faraday rotation measurements. However, the use of FIR sources in Thomson scattering measurements has only recently been employed [1, 2], CW FIR laser scattering provides a nonperturbing method of determining the ω and k spectra of the nonthermal density fluctuations existing in both laboratory and fusion plasmas. In addition, it offers distinct advantages over the existing Thomson scattering systems which employ either microwave or CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser radiation sources.

articleTitle: Status of Submillimeter-Wave Thomson Scattering Ion Temperature Diagnostic Implementation in Alcator C
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The M.I.T. submillimeter-wave (SMM) Thomson scattering ion temperature diagnostic for the Alcator C tokamak is the first such implementation on a major plasma fusion machine. Successful measurement of the ion temperature using this technique will represent a major breakthrough for the determination of this critical parameter in present machines and planned demonstration reactors. The present implementation of this diagnostic makes use of state of the art high power, narrow linewidth SMM lasers [1] (like the 385 Jim D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O laser reported at this conference), a low noise Shottky barrier diode heterodyne receiver [2], and signal processing equipment. The simultaneous availability of this equipment will make possible, for the first time, the experimental test of the physical concepts involved in this diagnostic.

articleTitle: Minimum Far-Infrared Solar Brightness Temperature and Sunspot Activity
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Since 1971 we measured the absolute solar far-infrared brightness temperature with balloon-borne lamellar-grating interferometers in a series of flights [1-6] at the CNES balloon launching station in Aire/Adour, France. In Figure 1 we show the result of the last flight no. 10 of September 14, 1978 as an example. Our successful flights are listed in Table 1 including measured or extrapolated minimum solar brightness temperatures as well as daily and monthly sunspot numbers [7-9] as a measure of solar activity. Contrary to ref. [6] the minimum brightness temperatures listed are not corrected for the center-to-limb variation.

articleTitle: Moding Effects in Open Resonators with Aperture Coupling
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: It is well known <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">[1]</sup> that gaseous optical lasers show a reduction of output power as an effect of mode degeneracy for discrete separation of the end mirrors. This effect is also important when open-resonators, using two spherical mirrors, or one flat and one spherical mirror, with aperture coupling are used for measurement of such parameters as refractive index, absorption coefficient, dielectric properties and scattering cross-sections. In such a resonance system a set of modes may exist, designated by TEMp, l, q, where p is the number of radial field variations, l is the number of azimuthal field variations, and q is the number of standing wave maxima between the mirrors. For a symmetrical circular input coupling aperture l = O. The system becomes resonant for a particular mode when the mirror separation D is equal to an integral number of half-wavelengths of that mode. Different modes have slightly different wavelengths.

articleTitle: Performance of Wideband Receiving Devices with Josephson Junctions
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In recent experiments, fairly high sensitivity of some Josephson junction receivers has been demonstrated (see reviews [1-3]). The theoretical analysis of their performance limits, however, has not been completed even within the framework of the simple and convenient “Resistively Shunted Junction” (RSJ) model (e.g., see [4]). The reason is that the best sensitivity can be achieved in the case most difficult for calculations, when the reduced signal source resistance R<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">E</inf> is comparable with the normal resistance of the Josephson junction [5], and the signal frequency f is of the order of the junction “characteristic frequency” f<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">C</inf>, typically from 100 to 500 GHz. The adequate analysis in the case of arbitrary R<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">E</inf> and f, occurs to be possible for wideband source-junction coupling with no essential reactances for all frequencies comparable with f. Following are the results of the analysis of noise performance limits for the most principal types of the Josephson-effect-based receivers (see [6] for details of calculations).

articleTitle: Temperature Dependence of the Water Vapor Continuum Absorption in the 3.5–4.0 m Region
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: An accurate and detailed knowledge of atmospheric transmission in and near the ir spectral windows is essential to the design, performance evaluation, and comparative testing of electro-optical (EO) systems. Of the many contributors to gaseous absorption in the atmosphere, water vapor is the most widespread spectrally and of greatest concern for many practical applications, especially for long-path high-visibility conditions. A major stumbling block to obtaining usable modeling predictions for EO, including high energy laser systems, is lack of an accurate data base for the water vapor continuum absorbtion in the 3-5 μm window. Although recent measurements by the Atmospheric Sciences Laboratory (ASL) have significantly improved the strength predictions and pressure dependence around 24°C, 1,2 the parameters needed to describe the temperature dependence have not been addressed. Lacking the needed data base, temperature scaling parameters measured under substantially higher temperature and pressure conditions than prevail in the normal atmosphere have been the only ones available for use in modeling the water vapor continuum absorption in the 3-5 μm window 3. The validity of using these temperature scaling parameters has been seriously questioned by the factor of 2 difference between predicted strengths and previous measurements performed by the ASL for 14.3 torr of water vapor air broadened to 1 atm. at 23°C 1 and 25°C 2 as well as an order of magnitude difference in the foreign-to-self broadening ratio 2. These discrepancies clearly expose the deficiencies of the present data base for modeling the 3-5 μm water vapor continuum and strengthen the support for investigating the temperature dependence.

articleTitle: Influence of a Strong Longitudinal Static Electric Field on Free Carrier Faraday Effect in An N-Type InSb at Room Temperature at Submillimeter-Wave Frequencies
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: With the aid of Kane's non-parabolic isotropic energy dispersion law [1], the motion of the conduction electron under the influence of electric field E and magnetic field B in the hydrodynamic approximation can be described by the following momentum transfer equation [2]: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">\frac{\mathrm{d{p\atop\rightarrow}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=e{\mathrm{E\atop\rightarrow}}+{\mathrm{v\atop\rightarrow}} \times {\mathrm{B\atop\rightarrow}}-\mathrm{m}*\nu_{e}{\mathrm{v\atop\rightarrow}} \tag{1}</tex> where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">{\mathrm{P\atop\rightarrow}}=m*{\mathrm{v\atop\rightarrow}}/\sqrt{1-(\mathrm{v/v}_{c})2}</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{c}}=\sqrt{\varepsilon g/(2m*)}</tex> Here, m∗ is the effective mass of an electron at the bottom of the conduction band. εg is the forbidden bandgap; <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">p</sup><sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">→</sub> is the momentum; e > 0 is electronic charge; v<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</sub> is the frequency of electron collision in which momentum is lost; and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">V</sup><sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">→</sub> is the electron velocity.

articleTitle: Frequency Stabilized Impatt Source in the Short Millimeter Wave Region
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A frequency stabilized IMPATT source for application to radio astronomy and plasma diagnostics has been developed. A harmonic mode of IMPATT operation is phase-locked through injection locking of the fundamental mode. An automatic frequency control system is used to stabilize the injection source of a Gunn device operating at the frequency desired.

articleTitle: Far Infrared Spectroscopy of In1-xGaXAsyP1-y
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The far infrared reflection spectrum of In<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1-x</inf>Ga<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">X</inf>As<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">y</inf>P<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1-y</inf> is analyzed for lattice effects. The main features of the spectrum are interpreted on the basis of an impurity mode model.

articleTitle: Water Vapor Absorption in the Submillimeter Spectral Region
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Water vapor absorption has been measured in the 5-100 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> spectral range under mid-latitude summer conditions. The experiment was performed using a photoacoustic cell with an optically pumped submillimeter laser.

articleTitle: Linear Theory of an Electron Cyclotron Maser Operating at the Fundamental
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We report the development of a general, linear theory of an electron cyclotron maser (ECM) operating at the fundamental. A set of analytic expressions, valid for all TE cavity modes, is derived for the starting current and frequency detuning using the Vlasov-Maxwell equations in the weakly relativistic limit. These results are applicable for an arbitrary electron velocity distribution as well as any longitudinal distribution of the RF field. It is shown that the starting current can be expressed in a simple form which contains the Fourier transform of the longitudinal field distribution. Analytic results are presented for specific longitudinal field variations, including uniform, sinusoidal, and Gaussian. It is found that the starting characteristics of an ECM are stongly influenced by the axial dependence of the RF field, but weakly affected by the velocity spread of the electron beam. The problem of multimode oscillation is treated rigorously in the linear theory by using a Slater expansion of the cavity field. Mode competition is investigated for higher order cavity modes and examples are presented. The results of this comprehensive analysis of ECM linear theory should be useful as a diagnostic of ECM performance and should facilitate comparison between theory and experiment.

articleTitle: First-Order Digital Analysis of Nondegenerate Josephson Paramps for MM Waves
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Nondegenerate Josephson paramps using point contacts are analyzed. A practical varactor model is employed for a first-order digital analysis of a realizable amplifier for 50 GHz. Presence of relatively high series inductance and low (≃10Ω) normal state resistance limit the bandwidth to less than MHz, qualitatively agreeing with reported experimental results.

articleTitle: Energy Losses from Building Envelopes by Heat Radiation and their Countermeasures
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications

articleTitle: A Temoo FIR Laser with Integrated Pump Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We describe a FIR Fabry Pérot resonator with metal mesh output coupler. The FIR laser gas CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F passively Q-switches the pump laser; thus the FIR radiation is pulsed. The beam geometry is good, we expect high efficiency and low noise.

articleTitle: Submillimetre Radiation at Continuous Photoexcitation of CdS Crystals
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The laser generation of submillimetre radiation in CdS crystals, excited by pulce radiation of a N<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-laser at room and nitrogen temperatures, was reported at a first time in our papers [1,2]. This radiation was explained by us as a result of transitions between exciton subbands, inverse population of them arises due to radiative Auger-recombination of excitons in their ground state. For many applications, in particular in spectroscopy, it is needed to have cw laser radiation tuning in the far infrared. Some indirect provements of the achievment of inverse population of exciton subbands in perfect monocrystals Cds and CdSe, excited by a mercury lamp at helium temperatures have been contained in our paper [3]. The aim of the work was to observe a submillimetre radiation in these conditions. As a result, we have obtained not only expected emmission by excitons, but also the submm radiation due to transitions between states of shallow impurities.

articleTitle: Design Considerations for a 240-GHz Gyromonotron
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: One of the most promising high-power, near-millimeter-wave (NMMW) sources at present is the cyclotron resonance maser (CRM), also known as the gyrotron. The attractiveness of this tube is due both to the high efficiency predicted for it theoretically [1] and to the remarkable performance of such tubes built by the Soviets. Examples of this performance are 1500 W cw at 9.9 mm [2] and 1.1 MW pulsed at 3 mm [3] with efficiencies around 10%. In a joint effort at the Harry Diamond Laboratories and the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), a gyrotron oscillator, or gyromonotron, is being built which will have an output power at 240 GHz of about 3.5 kW with an overall efficiency of 13%. Figure 1 is a schematic of the overall layout of the device. The highly uniform axial magnetic field required for the CRM interaction is to be produced by a superconducting magnet system available at NRL. Since the maximum magnetic field produced by this magnet is 60 kG, the minimum possible cyclotron harmonic, S, and the one chosen, was 2.

articleTitle: Very Longwavelength Lowpass Interference Filters
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The use of metallic mesh as the reflecting elements in interference filters for wavelengths longer than 50 μm is now well-established [1]. This paper discusses the design and production of low frequency pass filters specifically for use in Tokamak plasma diagnostics. The edges of the filters were specified at 4.3 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> and 6.3 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> (2325 μm and 1587 μm respectively). In addition an approach to broadbandpass filters using highpass and lowpass combinations is discussed.

articleTitle: Uniform Transmission Si Fabry Perot Couplers for Optically Pumped FIR Lasers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: An ideal output coupler for CW optically pumped FIR laser must present : i) a low adjustable and uniform FIR transmission coefficient (≲ 0.1), ii) a weak absorption at FIR wavelengths, iii) a good reflection at the pump wavelength. The condition of uniform transmission is essential to obtain a slowly diverging FIR output beam. Hybrid couplers which satisfy in part the properties i), ii), iii), have been successfully developed beyond 100 μm [1], [2]. Different versions of Fabry-Perot (F-P) couplers have been recently proposed at shorter FIR wavelengths; a space fixed triple plate system specially designed for 70 μm [3] and a variable double wire-mesh interferometer [4]. We have realized a variable double silicon plate F-P coupler which fulfils the conditions i), ii), over a large FIR frequency range and avoids the damage caused by intense pump beams in mesh systems [5].

articleTitle: Intracavity Polarization Modulation in Optically Pumped Far-Infrared Lasers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A room temperature technique for modulating the plane of polarization of far-infrared (FIR) laser radiation is presented which is simple, lossless and has been demonstrated at high frequency (∼10 kHz).

articleTitle: Spectroscopy of the Lasing CH3OH Molecule
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The development of infrared lasers has had a significant impact on the study of vibrationally excited molecules. As a logical extrapolation of well known techniques, low power diode lasers are used instead of wideband sources and monochromators to provide absorption spectra with doppler limited resolution. The use of fixed frequency, medium and high power gas lasers relies on accidental near coincidences with particular absorption lines, which can be studied in great detail. One such technique is laser stark spectroscopy, where an electric field tunes the various M-components of the infrared transition into exact resonance with the laser, and where the use of a saturating beam and a counter propagating probe beam allows the resolution to go orders of magnitude beyond the doppler limit.

articleTitle: Sever Design for Gyrotron Traveling Wave Amplifiers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A multi-stage gyrotron amplifier is analyzed by the sever design computer program. A detailed study of sever loss is carried out for the TE modes in a simple cylindrical waveguide with one sever region. The space charge wave is ignored to observe the tendency of the sever loss. Results indicate that the characteristics of the gyrotron with a sever resemble those found in other TWT devices.

articleTitle: Submillimeter-Wave Properties of Thermospheric Rocket Plumes
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Observability of rocket plumes at thermospheric altitudes using high-resolution submillimeter-wave spectral line radiometry has been investigated [1]. Calculations that include collisional, radiative, and flow effects indicate that low-lying rotational transitions of plume species, particularly water vapor, have sufficient optical depth and spatial extent for satellite applications.

articleTitle: Guided Synchronous Millimeter and Submillimeter Modes on Planar Structures
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: One of today's challenges for future sub-millimeter wave technology is the development of suitable guided structures for device integration and signal processing. We have made initial theoretical studies concerning the feasibility of propagating submillimeter waves along semiconductor interfaces as interface electromagnetic waves (IEM). In particular, our efforts have been directed toward structures in which synchronous propagation with millimeter waves might permit parametric interaction through a nonlinear material dielectric constant.

articleTitle: Unstable Resonator Laser Performance at Several Near-Millimeter Wavelengths
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The utility of unstable-resonator (UR) laser cavities has been amply demonstrated with visible and infrared lasers. Extensive analysis of their performance and characteristics has been conducted at these wavelengths. However, in the near-millimeter wave region (NMMW - roughly 0.3 to 3 mm) relatively little has been done [1, 2, 3]. Nevertheless their ability to provide compact dimensions, excellent energy conversion, and good mode control has been demonstrated. This paper presents additional results dealing primarily with C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F at 605 GHz and C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup>H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F at 246 GHz, but also with performance with other gaseous gain media.

articleTitle: CD3F Optically Pumped Near Millimeter Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We have recently reported laser action in fully deuterated methyl fluoride on 12 lines in the wavelength range 155.6 to 384.7 μm [1]. The two strongest lines at 206 μm and 247.5 μm produce milliwatt level cw laser action in an unoptimized hole-coupled cavity. Some additional characteristics of the laser, the observation of several more lines which extend the range of operation of CD<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F to 1.485 mm, and some transition assignments are reported in this paper.

articleTitle: Quantitative Line and Band Shape Studies with a Pressure-Scanning Millimeter Wave Dispersion Spectrometer
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A pressure-scanning spectrometer was especially developed to measure the numerous spectroscopic parameters (line: position, strength, self and foreign broadened width, shift, shape; band and continuum: absolute intensity, shape) of oxygen and water vapor, which are central to the calculation of transfer and emission characteristics exhibited by moist air in the EHF (30–300 GHz) band.

articleTitle: Effect of Geometrical and Multiple Image Interactions on Tunneling and I-V Characteristics of Infrared Point-Contact Detectors
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In this paper we wish to report some recent theoretical results on the effect of the image and multiple image interactions on the tunneling and rectification characteristics of metallic cat-whisker diodes used in precision determinations of infrared laser frequencies [1-3]. The structure is an ultra fine metal tip (< 1 μm radius) in contact with a flat metal anode separated by a distance of the order of 10-40 Å. It has been suggested that the diode configuration can be considered a MOM planar tunneling junction described by Simmons theory [1,4]. The authors have questioned the applicability of the Simmons MOM model, based upon planar geometry, to the cat-whisker diode configuration and refined the model, using somewhat different solid state mechanisms [5-7]. This new model includes a thermally enhanced field induced tunneling process to explain the nonlinearity of the devices and a new rectification mechanism, independent of material asymmetry, which takes into account explictly the geometrical shape of the electrodes [8-10]. That is, the actual curvature of the tip gives rise to a nonuniform electric field across the metal-vacuum-metal (MVM) or metal-oxide-metal junction. As a consequence of the nonuniform field distribution, there is a different tunneling barrier for forward and reverse bias which leads to rectification [9].

articleTitle: Reliable Far Infrared Photoconductivity Method to Identify a Variety of Residual Donors in Epitaxial GaAs
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The 1s to 2p(m=–1) transition of different hydrogen-like donors can be resolved in high magnetic fields because of the central-cell shift of the energy level of the 1s state. Continuation of the work of Stillman, Stradling, and others.

articleTitle: Phase Shifting at 94 GHz using Bulk Crystals
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In recent years there has been increased interest in electrically-controlled phase shifters in the near-millimeter spectral region for use in phased array radar systems. Past work in millimeter-wave phase shifters has made use of the electrically controlled conductivity of semiconductors such as silicon. The semiconductor can be used in the form of a dielectric waveguide, with carriers injected along one wall (either electrically [1] or optically [2]), or the sample (in the form of a diode) can be inserted along one wall of a hollow metallic waveguide [3]. In these experiments large phase shifts (on the order of 50–100 degrees) have been observed, but the devices are limited in speed by the carrier recombination time (10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−6</sup>–10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−5</sup> seconds) and are complicated structurally.

articleTitle: Results of a Survey on Calibration Standards Requirements
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: As the field of infrared and millimeter wave research grows, there is an increasing need for commonly accepted power and energy calibration standards. For example, both manufacturers and customers would benefit from the availability of appropriate standards for characterizing sources and detectors. Until the time when the national standards laboratories become more fully involved in this effort, it is particularly important to foster the exchange of information on this subject among researchers. It seems that the series of international conferences that are so well attended by workers in the field of infrared and millimeter waves offers an ideal forum in which this information can be shared. The discussion group on calibration standards at the San Juan meeting and T. G. Blaney's poster at the Guildford meeting set a trend that should be continued. The calibration poster session at this conference has been organized in order to promote the exchange of information about quasioptical (free-space) techniques for power and energy calibration in the infrared and millimeter wavelength range.

articleTitle: Calibration of Power and Energy Meters for the Far Infrared/Near-Millimeter Wave Spectral Region
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Power and energy measurements in the FIR/near-millimeter-wave region of the spectrum have acquired an increasing importance as growth in technology and experimentation in this area progresses. Relatively inexpensive detectors and power meters exist that are designed for visible and near-infrared wavelengths, but accurate calibration factors in the FIR for such instruments are lacking. While it is not the purpose of this research to establish standards for absolute power and energy measurements, useful information interchange may be accomplished utilizing devices now commonly available in many laboratories, providing that calibration factors for these devices are established.

articleTitle: High-Intensity CO2 Laser Pumping of a 12CH3F Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We report the observation of 21 new, efficient far-infrared (FIR) Raman laser lines in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F. These new lines are excited by high-intensity, off-resonant CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> TEA laser radiation in a waveguide laser system. Previous surveys of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F with high-power CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> TEA lasers have achieved strong, efficient laser emission at only two wave lengths, 496.1 μm (Refs. 1 and 2) and 192.8 μm.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> Fetterman et al.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup> have obtained some additional lines in CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F, demonstrating the importance of off-resonant optical pumping in pulsed FIR lasers. In their studies, as well as others, CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> TEA laser excitation of molecular gases has produced FIR radiation with a maximum of 1-2 GHz off resonance.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5, 6</sup> We recently reported<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">7</sup> fifteen new Raman lines in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F utilizing a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> pump intensity of 10 - 20 MW/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. By using an oscillator-amplifier CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser system, we have increased the pump intensity to 40 - 60 MW/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. This has resulted in the observation of six additional lines with offsets as large as 20 GHz.

articleTitle: Anomalous Absorption in Random Small Particle Composites
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The far-infrared absorption of composite systems consisting of small metal particles with radii in the 100Å - 1μm range in an insulating host has been measured over 4-200 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup>. The magnitude of the absorption was substantially larger than predicted by simple electromagnetic theory. An intriguing result found in previous investigations<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1,2,3</sup> of the far infrared absorption in small-particle composite systems is that the magnitude of the absorption is considerably larger than what is predicted by classical electromagnetic theory.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4,5,6</sup> Explanations which have been proposed for this effect include absorption in dielectric coatings on the particles,<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">7</sup> absorption within clusters of particles,<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">8</sup> and changes in the properties of the metal particles arising from size quantization of the electronic energy levels.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1,9</sup> In this paper we present the results of an experimental study of far infrared absorption in small particle composite systems.

articleTitle: Detection of NMMW Radiation with Mercury Cadmium Telluride
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The need for semiconductors with a variable valence to conduction bandgap has led to the study of various ternary compounds. Among these, [Hg,Cd]Te has been developed for use as detectors [1] and lasers [2,3] in the 8 to 14-μm spectral region. We report the first observation of hot-electron photoconductive detection of near-millimeter wave (NMMW) radiation using [Hg,Cd]Te.

articleTitle: The Far Infrared Complex Reflectivity of Semiconductor GaTe
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The purpose of this presentation is to report the experimental far infrared polarized complex reflection (amplitude r and phase ⊘) spectra of single crystal GaTe using a dispersive Michelson interferometer [1] as a contribution to the understanding of its lattice dynamics. Further, the results obtained are unique in that the dispersive instrument is able to measure samples as small as 4-10 mm diameter, which is particularly suited for GaTe crystals. Other workers [2-5] use different optical techniques and seem to require much larger sample sizes.

articleTitle: Calibration of a Fourier Transform Spectrometer using Ln-Cooled Microwave Absorber
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: During the past five years, the measurement of electron cyclotron emission (ECE) from tokamaks has developed from the initial efforts into a diagnostic of generally recognized importance. Fourier transform spectrometers (FTS) incorporating the fast-scanning Martin-Puplett interferometer are widely used to make these measurements. Spectral scans of the second harmonic line in the ECE spectrum that are made with this instrument lead straightforwardly to the determination of the shape of the electron temperature profile. The determination of the profile shape involves a relative spectral calibration of the instrument that is made by measuring the spectrum of a known broadband calibration source. Achieving an absolute calibration is more difficult. Usually, the necessary multiplicative factor for converting the measured relative profile into absolute values of electron temperature has been obtained by normalizing the profiles to those that are obtained with a Thomson scattering electron temperature diagnostic. However, it would be more satisfactory if the instrument could be absolutely calibrated by a means that is independent of any other plasma diagnostic. This paper reports the preliminary results that have been obtained in an effort to absolutely calibrate the FTS system that is being operated by the University of Maryland group on the PLT tokamak at Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory.

articleTitle: Far Infrared Spectroscopy of Polar Molecules in a Non Polar Solvent and Dielectric Relaxation
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The knowledge of the frequency dependence of the permittivity of polar liquids and of solutions of polar molecules in non polar solvents can give an insight into the relative role of dipole-dipole coupling with respect to other molecular interactions. By power reflectometry in the microwave frequency range, Finsy and Van Loon [1] have shown the importance of the dipole-dipole coupling (through the “dielectric friction” described by Nee and Zwanzig [2] for 1,1,1 trichloro-ethane (T. C.E.) in solution in cyclohexane.

articleTitle: Josephson Mixer Receiver for 300 GHz
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A mixer receiver for 300 GHz incorporating a permanent point contact Josephson junction, a cooled Schottky barrier multiplier and a cooled Ga As FET if amplifier is described. The system is tunable over 100 GHz, and preliminary tests indicate a DSB noise temperature of 500 K.

articleTitle: Far Infrared Emission Diagnostics on Tokamak Alcator C
