publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Measurements of electron cyclotron radiation on the Tokamak Alcator C show a degree of polarization, extraordinary to ordinary mode, of approximately 2 to 1, similar to Alcator A. A rapid scan Michelson interferometer provides up to 32 interferograms per plasma pulse and transformed spectra are available immediately afterward. Electron temperature profiles are determined from the second harmonic emission in each spectrum.

articleTitle: A Twin Optically-Pumped Far-Infrared CH3OH Laser for Plasma Diagnostics
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A twin optically-pumped far-infrared CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH laser has been constructed for use in plasma diagnostics. The anti-symmetric doublet due to the Raman-type resonant two-photon transition is reproducibly observed at 118.8 μm. The doublet separation can be tunable upto 5.3 MHz by changing the pump offset frequency. Some preliminary performances of this laser for the modulated interferometer are described.

articleTitle: Improved Submillimeter Schottky Diodes using Front Surface Metallization
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The high frequency behaviour of Schottky diode mixers is discussed. Improved performance is predicted for diodes with reduced skin effect resistance due to front surface metallization. The performance of diodes fabricated in this manner is described.

articleTitle: Spectral Diffuse Ir-Reflectivity of Small Particles
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: For the measurement of the spectral diffuse ir-reflectivity of small particles, fibres and technical surfaces at wavelengths between 2.5 μm and 30 μm we have modified an ir spectrophotometer (Beckman IR 12) replacing its detector system by an axial ellipsoidal 406 mm mirror and a pyroelectric TGS detector (Heimann GmbH, Wiesbaden) in one of its focuses (Fig. 1). The sample of 20 mm diameter is placed in the other focus. It is exchanged at small spectral intervals with a reflectivity standard of the same size by a mechanical switch. The ratio of the reflectivity of the sample versus that of the standard as a function of the wavenumber is evaluated by a microprocessor and plotted.

articleTitle: The Importance of Geometry, Field, and Temperature on Tunneling and Rectification Behavior in Infrared Point-Contact Diodes of Identical and Disimilar Metals
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In this talk we present some recent theoretical results on the study of tunneling and current-voltage (I-V) characteristics of metallic cat whisker point-contact diodes. These point-contact devices, which currently have the fastest response times (∼< 2 orders of magnitude) of all infrared and optical detectors (e.g., Josephson tunneling devices, Schottky barrier diodes, etc.) [1], have applications to precision frequency measurements [1-3] as well as in quantum electronics and solid-state physics [4], including infrared studies of superconductivity [5]. The structure is made of an ultra-fine metal tip, comparable to those used in field emission (i.e., ∼10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−</sup> 2 - 1 μm radius) in contact with a flat metal anode. A fundamental application of these devices has been the most precise and accurate determination of the velocity of light [1-3,6,7].

articleTitle: Density Profiles in Tokamaks from Electron Cyclotron Radiation Spectra
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Measurement of the line shape of optically thick and optically thin lines in the electron cyclotron radiation spectrum emitted by a tokamak plasma may yield both electron temperature and density profiles. An algorithm is discussed.

articleTitle: Far-Infrared Laser Spectroscopy of Water Vapor and Liquid Water
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We have used a far infrared (FIR) optically pumped laser to measure both the reflection and transmission of liquid water and the absorption by water vapor of radiation in the spectral region betwen 8.22 and 175.7 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup>. The pumped laser is a unique feature of our measurements. The high power of this device gives a signal-to-noise ratio which is superior to that available from broadband FIR sources. The optical data for liquid water were used to determine the complex refractive index n-ik [1]. Data for measured absorption by water vapor were compared with calculations of predicted absorption based on the line shape formula given by Gross. Our measured absorptions are in excess of the theoretical values at each of the laser frequencies and at all pressures.

articleTitle: Intracavity Double Resonance on Optically Pumped Submm Lasers: Asymmetry Splittings in Methyl Alcohol
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Optically pumped submillimeter lasers provide useful and sometime exclusive information on the spectroscopy of the active medium molecules. For instance the Stark effect on highly excited levels of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F and CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH was recently investigated (1). A double resonance experiment on the active molecules of a HCOOH laser was for the first time reported in [2]. In the present communication we report the first observation of an intracavity double resonance effect on an optically pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH FIR laser. Due to the complexity of the structure and to the liberality of the selection rules, FIR laser emission from CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH has been observed at more than one hundred different wavelengths. Methyl alcohol plays also an important role in molecular spectroscopy since it constitutes a test for theoretical and experimental investigations of a molecule with hindered internal rotation.

articleTitle: Electron Beam Fabrication of Submillimeter Schottky Diodes
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Submillimeter Schottky barrier diodes of submicron dimensions have been produced using a specially developed electron beam lithography technique. The effect on diode parasitics of different shaped anodes has been investigated. DC and RF performance data will be presented.

articleTitle: Nonlinear Multimode Formulation of Electron Cyclotron Maser Oscillators
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: This paper presents the nonlinear formulation for the problem of the electron maser in an overmoded cavity.

articleTitle: Prospects for a Tunable, High Power CH3F Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Laser pumping of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F with high intensity radiation [1] from a grating tuned CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> TEA has produced Raman far-infrared (FIR) emission with pump offsets as large as 20 GHz. Analysis of these results suggests that a nearly continuously tunable FIR laser could be constructed if a tunable pump source were utilized. This system would be similar in principle to the tunable FIR sources using the diatomic molecules HF [2] and HCL [3]. A tunable CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F laser, however, would have the advantages of a higher overall efficiency and narrower bandwidth. We present a theoretical analysis which predicts the tuning behavior of such a tunable CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F laser. Data previously taken [1] with a grating tuned CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> TEA laser are used to determine the necessary pump intensity and the operating pressure.

articleTitle: Dispersion in a Laser Pumped Molecular Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The dispersion equations have been derived for two laser fields of arbitrary intensity interacting with a homogeneously broadened, three-level molecular system. Good agreement is obtained between theoretical and experimental results for frequency detuning in a 385 μm, D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O laser and a 496 μm CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F laser.

articleTitle: Infrared Generation by Nonlinear Optical Means in Hg0.77Cd0.23Te
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Hg<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1-X</inf>Cd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">X</inf>Te is an alloy semiconductor which has found widespread use in photoconductive and photovoltaic infrared detectors. Thus methods for preparing homogeneous single crystals of controlled composition (x-value) and purity are well established. Many of the same properties which make it useful for infrared detection can also be exploited in nonlinear optics experiments [1]. Those of interest depend upon interaction of incident photons from a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser with free electrons when the sample is immersed in a magnetic field. Three such third order nonlinear optical effects are the spin-flip Raman laser, resonant four-photon mixing, and optical phase conjugation. A second order nonlinear optical effect of interest is far infrared generation by difference frequency mixing. To maximize the scattering cross section, the composition is adjusted during growth to that value such that the optical absorption edge at 4°K coincides with the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser wavelength. The appropriate composition is Hg<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.77</inf>Cd<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.23</inf>Te. At this composition the free electron effective mass ratio is small, ∼0.0095 so that the spin-level splitting factor (g-value) is large, ∼80. This also gives rise to a large scattering cross-section. Furthermore, conduction band nonparabolicity effects due to the small forbidden energy gap give rise to other, non-resonant, nonlinearities. Each of these nonlinear optical effects is discussed below.

articleTitle: CO2 Laser-Induced Multiphoton Dissociation of CH3CCl3 in the Vapor Phase
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In practical applications of multi-photon dissociation (MPD) collisional interference [1, 2] may not be avoidable. Therefore, we addressed this problem by a study on the MPD of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>CCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> in the vapor phase. This molecule has been recently investigated in a molecular beam experiment [3].

articleTitle: Near-Millimeter Wave Emission Assignments for 1,1-Difluoroethylene
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Refinements in the instrumentation of a diode laser heterodyne spectrometer permit the rapid and routine measurement of infrared absorptions lying within 6.5 GHz of a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser emission to a precision and accuracy well within 10 MHz. Several hundred lines of the spectrum of 1,1-difluoroethylene (F<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>C=CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>) have been measured and identified by fitting to an asymmetric-top Hamiltonian with standard deviations of 6 MHz. Near-millimeter wave assignments can be made from the improved molecular constants.

articleTitle: Beam Quality Studies for Intense Beam Free Electron Lasers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Free electron laser (FEL) experiments conducted to date using intense beams have incorporated cold-cathode, foil-less diodes for beam generation [1,2,3]. Although such beams have been sufficient to demonstrate the basic characteristics of stimulated backscattering, quantitative interpretation of the interaction has suffered from a lack of information concerning beam quality.

articleTitle: CH3F Laser Pumped with a Continuously Tunable, Multi-Atmosphere CO2 Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: While very powerful, narrow bandwidth, pulsed FIR lasers are being constructed for plasma diagnosis it is striking to observe that a very small number of rotational transitions of very few molecules are under investigation. This comes from the fact that many conditions must be fulfilled to obtain efficient pulsed FIR laser emission [1]. One of the most important is that the molecule used must be quite simple in order that the ground absorbing state contains a good fraction of the population of the molecules and that FIR reabsorption from rotational transitions of the ground state be negligible. Furthermore, a near coincidence is required between an absorption line of the molecule and an emission line of the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-TEA laser. If the first condition is unavoidable the second one might be circumvented by using a continuously tunable multi-atmosphere CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser. Then it should be possible to pump a molecule which would be a good candidate on most of its vibrational rotational absorption lines. Let us take for example the CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F molecule which has only been pumped via two of its absorption lines by the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-TEA laser (the Q (12) and P (32) of the C-F strech mode). The Q branch of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F is situated in a part of the spectrum contained between the 9P18 and 9P36 line of the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> molecule. In this branch, there are nearly forty CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F absorption lines which could produce as much efficient millimeter and submillimeter lines. Some other lines in the P and R branches are also accessible with other parts of the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser spectrum, but they would lead to the same FIR lines.

articleTitle: High Power Pulsed C13H3F Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Far infrared (FIR) and millimeter-wave source and receiver development has grown significantly in recent years. The existence of atmospheric windows around the millimeter wavelength has stimulated interest in areas such as communications and radar design. The advantages to be gained by the use of the FIR in fusion plasma diagnostics is already being realized and should prove increasingly important in the future.

articleTitle: A Michelson Interferometer for Tokamak Far-Infrared Fourier — Transform Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Far-infrared Fourier-transform spectroscopy [1] is now a standard diagnostic to measure the electron cyclotron emission from Tokamak plasmas. Various efforts have been made to improve this diagnostic [2, 3]. We will present at the conference the modifications which we made on the original N.P.L. design of the cube interferometer. Special attention has been given to the data acquisition system. The far-infrared interferometer has been equipped with a visible interferometer to monitor the mirror displacement. A special electronics unit has been built, which has 3 essential functions - control the mirror displacement - digitize the analog interferogram for storage into a 4 K buffer memory - provide a permanent reading of the stored interferograms. This part of the system was found extremely useful and well adapted to Tokamak conditions. We will also present results of measurements made on the TFR device.

articleTitle: An Airborne Far-Infrared Spectrometer for Astronomical Observations
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A Fabry-Perot spectrometer for airborne observation of astronomical spectral lines has been designed for use in the 50 to 200μm region of the far-infrared. In this wavelength range lie fine structure lines from atoms and ions, and rotational transitions of light molecules such as hydrides. In a one arcminute beam a telescope will receive a far-infrared flux from the brightest fine structure lines of up to 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−15</sup> W cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−2</sup>, with a Doppler width of 1 part in 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sup>. The study of these lines is discussed in a companion paper [1].

articleTitle: Gyrotron Developments at Varian and Topics for Further Development
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Cyclotron resonance coupling between microwave fields and an electron beam in vacuum is the basis for a family of microwave generators. This type of coupling has the advantage that both the beam and the associated microwave structures can have dimensions large compared to a wavelength. This allows the generation of orders of magnitude higher power output at a given wavelength than can be produced with conventional microwave tubes. The microwave interaction circuit can take the form of a single resonant cavity. This results in an oscillator device which has been called a gyrotron (1), (2). An amplifier can be made by using two cavities each operating below the oscillation threshold, where an input microwave signal is used to modulate the beam in one cavity and output power is removed from the modulated beam using the second cavity. By analogy this has been called a gyroklystron. Still another variation of cyclotron resonance coupling has been called a gyro traveling wave amplifier (gyro TWT). In that case a continuous waveguide is used for distributed interaction between the electron beam and a traveling wave.

articleTitle: Computer Simulation of Three-Dimensional Pyroelectric IR Detectors
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: An algorithm given in [1] is revised and realized on computer for calculating the performance of thin pyroelectric IR detectors. The detector considered consists of a thin circular crystal plate of radius γ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> and thickness d, coated with circular surface electrodes of radius γ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf>, and mounted on a shallow cylindrical substrate of inner radius γ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf> and thickness d<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf> so that the detector is effectively free-bearing. (Fig. 1).

articleTitle: Large Electron-Hole Drop in Germanium
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The strain-confined large electron-hole drop (LEHD) in germanium is characterized by its long life, a well-defined excitonic atmosphere and a large work function. These characteristics are confirmed through millimeter wave dimensional resonance and far-infrared attenuation.

articleTitle: Electron Density Measurements by Deflection of a Far Infrared Laser Beam
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Electron densities in the range 3 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">14</sup> < N<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">e</inf> < 6 × 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sup>cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−3</sup> have been determined in a laser-initiated vacuum arc using a novel far infrared method. The density, and its spatial distribution, were determined by measuring deflections of a beam from a CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH laser at 119 and 171 micrometers.

articleTitle: FIR Collective Scattering from the UCLA Microtor Tokamak
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The anomalous transport and energy loss observed in present toroidal magnetic fusion confinement devices may be due to low frequency microturbulence [1]. One way of studying such turbulence has been to scatter microwave or CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser radiation from small-scale density fluctuations [2-8]. As long as the scattering parameter α = 1/kλ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">D</inf> ≃ λ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">O</inf>/4Πλ sin(θ/2) ≳ 1, one obtains information about collective fluctuations. The problem with both CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> and microwave scattering is that if one satisfies the abovementioned criterion it is not possible to simultaneously provide a localized scattering measurement and good wavenumber resolution. On the other hand, FIR laser scattering is ideally suited to magnetic fusion parameters and easily provides spatial resolution Δx ≃ 1.5-3 cm while providing wavenumber resolution Δk ≳ 3 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> FWHM. An additional bonus arises from the ease of changing incident laser wavelength, thereby increasing the range of instability wavenumbers which can be investigated (k ≃ 4Πsin(θ/2)/λ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">O</inf>).

articleTitle: Observations of Far-Infrared Fine Structure Lines in the Interstellar Medium
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Fine structure lines in the far-infrared have many simple properties that make them useful tools for diagnosing astrophysical plasmas. The line ratios are sensitive and accurate probes of density, elemental abundances, and ionization structure; also, line shapes and Doppler shifts have proven handy in studies of gross dynamics of H II regions and galaxies. These lines have several analytical and practical advantages over spectral features in the optical and radio regions for measuring certain parameters of ionized regions.

articleTitle: Submillimeter Guided Wave Experiments with Polyethylene Slab Waveguide
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Recently, techniques of integrated optics have been vigorously developed in the optical and microwave regions. However, these techniques are little extended to the submillimeter-wave region. In this paper, the attenuation and phase constants of dielectric slab waveguide as the basic guide structure of the submillimeter integrated circuits are measured by using the “sliding metal grating coupler” at λ<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</inf>=337μm, and also the examination about accuracy and reliability of their measured values are sufficiently performed. Moreover, the radiation loss due to their bend is experimentally discussed.

articleTitle: Far Infrared Studies on CdSe and CdSe:Cr
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: II—VI compounds have a wide variety of applications and CdSe in particular has been studied for its application as a nonlinear element in the frequency conversion of gas laser radiation. Lattice dynamics of wurtzite structure has been studied (1). The presence of Cadmium makes neutron diffraction difficult to apply to CdSe.

articleTitle: Millimeter Spectroscopy in Giant Atoms
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Rydberg atoms are very excited atomic states prepared close to the ionization limit. They have huge dimensions at atomic scale, very long lifetimes and very large electric dipole matrix elements for transitions connecting nearby levels and falling in the millimeter range. Moreover, they are very easy to detect. These features make these species very attractive for new developments in microwave and far-infrared technology.

articleTitle: Resolution Limits in Tokamak Far Infrared Fourier Transform Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The measurement of the electron cyclotron emission from Tokamak discharges is a powerful method to investigate the electron distribution function. Among the different methods currently used to measure this emission [ 1] Fourier Transform Spectroscopy [2] is now a routine diagnostic used on several Tokamaks throughout the world. For a Maxwellian distribution function this method gives the radial profile of the electron temperature and its time variation [3, 4]. In view of the difficulties encountered with other diagnostic methods (such as Thomson scattering or soft -X ray measurements) to obtain this information it appears that Fourier transform spectroscopy has still a rather promising future and we want to analyze here the limits of the method both in nowadays and to-morrow's Tokamaks.

articleTitle: A Fabry-Perot Interferometer for Plasma Diagnostics
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Electron cyclotron emission is an important diagnostic tool in the study of tokamak plasmas. Using fast-scan Michelson interferometry, electron temperature profiles in tokamak plasmas with typical time and space resolutions of 10 ms and 5 cm respectively can be obtained [1]. Experiments at MIT on ALCATOR [2] have shown that it is possible to measure the emission at fixed frequencies with time and space resolutions of 1 ms and 2 cm using a Fabry-Perot interferometer. In the present paper, a Fabry-Perot interferometer is described which can be operated in both a static and a scanning mode. In the static mode it allows study of the plasma emission with a time resolution of about 1 μs (limited by the detector bandwidth) with a spatial resolution of 4 cm. In the scanning mode of operation, the second harmonic of the cyclotron emission from a typical tokamak (DITE) covering the range 120 to 170 GHz can be measured in 2.5 ms with a resolution of about 5 GHz (spatial resolution about 4 cm).

articleTitle: Dielectric-Clad Circuit TWT with TM01 Mode Interaction
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The TM<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">01</inf> mode of the dielectric-clad cylindrical waveguide circuit was analyzed to obtain the dispersion and interaction impedance for TWT analysis. The Pierce parameters were modified for analysis with intense relativistic electron beams. A computer code was written for the complete analysis of gain versus frequency including launching loss and sever regions. The results indicate the possibility of achieving bandwidth exceeding one octave and peak power levels of one gigawatt near 600 kilovolts using this simple interaction structure.

articleTitle: Final Report of the Near-Millimeter Wave Study Subpanel on Atmospheric Propagation
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The desire to “see” through limited visibility environments such as fogs, clouds, and smokes has recently motivated substantial interest in that portion of the electromagnetic spectrum having wavelengths near 1 mm. This region appears to offer an attractive compromise between the high resolution capabilities of infrared radiation and the low loss propagation characteristics of microwaves. The technology base for such millimeter/submillimeter wavelengths is, however, extremely limited.

articleTitle: Prospects of Developing Multi-Megawatt Gyrotrons for Bulk Heating of Controlled Thermonuclear Reactors
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Nearly 20 years have elapsed since basic theoretical and experimental studies confirmed the validity of the electron cyclotron maser gain mechanism. The leading effort in exploiting this knowledge to develop a new class of millimeter-wave oscillators at uniquely high power levels was made in the Soviet Union. This effort led to the announcement in 1974 of efficient kilowatt-level, CW gyrotron oscillators at millimeter and submillimeter wavelengths [1], and in 1978 to the announcement of megawatt long-pulse devices at 3 and 6.7 mm wavelengths [2]. An effort in the U.S. has also been set into motion to produce gyrotron oscillators for fusion plasma heating experiments. Gyrotrons producing kJ pulses of energy have been developed by Varian Associates at 28 GHz [3], and by the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) at 35 GHz [4]. The latter device is presently being deployed in electron-cyclotron-resonance-heating (ECRH) experiments.

articleTitle: The Donor Minus Ion in Semiconductors
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: At low temperature, some electrons from the conduction band may recombine with neutral donors to produce isolated D<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−</sup> centers. The binding energy of this hydrogen-minus-like center is in the submillimeter range. Excited Rydberg-like states have been observed but only in the presence of a magnetic field.

articleTitle: The Orotron — A Millimeter Wave Generator Based on the Smith — Purcell Effect
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The orotron [1], ledatron [2], and diffraction radiation generator [3] are electron-tube devices that generate millimeter and submillimeter wave radiation by means of the Smith-Purcell effect. We have shown [4] that these devices are special cases of a general class of Smith-Purcell free-electron lasers considered by Wachtel [5]. The essential difference between these Smith-Purcell lasers and other free-electron lasers [6] is that in the former the electrons are bunched by a longitudinal rf electric field but in the latter they are bunched by a transverse magnetic field.

articleTitle: A New Method of Reflection Dispersive Fourier Transform Spectroscopy of Near-Opaque Liquids and Solids
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A transparent window is introduced in the sample arm of a dispersive, two beam interferometer to act as a reference optical starting position of the recorded interferograms to eliminate micrometer back-lash error, and to give reproducible phase information leading to determination of precise absorption and refraction spectra.

articleTitle: Characteristics of the D2O Laser Emission at 50, 66, 83, 111 and 116 μm
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O laser pumped by the 9P(32) CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser line was previously known to be a strong 66 μm source showing some substantially smaller contributions at 50, 83 and 116 μm /1/. We report on a study of the individual emission characteristics of the known lines which led to the discovery of an additional efficient line at 111 μm. The experiments were performed with the oscillator described at the CIRP2 conference /2/: the resonator, formed by a concave mirror (R=6m) and a copper mesh (grid constant g=25 μm), is stabilized and tunable. Its total length can be chosen between 5 and 100 cm. The FIR radiation is reflected out of the laser by one of a selection of Reststrahlen crystals, chosen according to the wavelength region being investigated /3/. In the experiments reported here, the D<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O vapour was axially pumped in a double pass By a 1 Joule, 20mm diameter, multimode TEA-CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser beam. Relative energy measurements (such as the dependence on pressure, and on resonator tuning) were made with a pyroelectric detector in the integrating mode, total energy measurements by means of a calorimeter. FIR pulse forms were recorded with a Ge:Ga detector cooled to 4 K. The pump pulse was monitored with a photon-drag detector.

articleTitle: Operating Characteristics of a 35 GHz Gyromonotron
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Results of experiments on the characteristics of a single cavity gyrotron oscillator are presented. The device produces 150 KW, has an efficiency ∼ 30%, a pulse length ∼10 msec, and a measured line width of less than 1.5 MHz. In this paper we describe experiments with a gyromonotron operating at 35 GHz with the output radiation in the TE<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">O1</inf> (circular) mode. Of principal interest in these experiments was the investigation of the basic operation of the device as well as two methods of efficiency optimization: the tapering of the cavity walls or of the applied magnetic field. Additionally, it was desired to produce a device suitable for ECH experiments, which requires a pulse length of at least 10 ms.

articleTitle: Near-Millimeter-Wave Polarizing Wire Grid Fabrication and Evaluation
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The wavelengths in the near-millimeter wavelength region (NMMW — roughly 0.3 to 3 mm) are sufficiently small that the conventional microwave fundamental-mode waveguide techniques are difficult to implement and are often of limited effectiveness. Quasi-optical components are frequently employed to overcome these difficulties. Free-standing planar one-dimensional wire grids show promise, based on their strong polarizing properties, in the fabrication of many such components. In this paper we discuss a straight-forward method of fabrication of one-dimensional wire grids that has been employed on a normal machine shop lathe to produce grids of sufficient quality for many NMMW applications. Examination of their mechanical quality and NMMW performance is also presented.

articleTitle: IR-Properties of the Atmosphere Relevant to Energy Losses of Buildings Caused by Heat Radiation
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In order to estimate the reduction of heat losses of buildings by irreflecting coatings on windows, walls and roofs we need detailed information on long-time local atmospheric thermal irradiance.

articleTitle: Direct Narrow line Tuning of a High Power CO2 Pump Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A high power, narrow line CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> pump laser for submillimeter laser applications has been constructed by direct grating tuning of an unstable resonator oscillator and injection tuning to a single longitudinal mode. The oscillator produces 200-400 joule pulses on the 9R(22) line with a line width of less than 20 MHz.

articleTitle: A New General Purpose, Variable Thickness, Variable Temperature, Liquid Cell for Fourier Transform and Laser Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We have constructed a general purpose, variable pathlength, variable temperature liquid cell which removes defocussing and converging effects in millimeter and submillimeter wave Fourier transform and laser spectroscopy of liquids. The liquid thickness can be varied continuously from 0 to 25 mm allowing absorption spectra of low loss liquids to be measured with high accuracy. The liquid cell (except for the liquid compartment) can be evacuated together with the interferometer, increasing the signal-to-noise ratio.

articleTitle: Design of the Gyrotron Traveling-Wave Amplifier with Te-11 Mode
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A gyrotron traveling wave amplifier was designed for high gain experiments with the dominant circular TE-11 mode. The calculated optimum circuit parameters are scaled to S-band for experiments to investigate performance characteristics of the future mm wave tube.

articleTitle: Water Vapor Attenuation of HF/CO2 Lasers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A resonant spectrophone has been used with a pulsed laser source to study water vapor attenuations of HF/CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> lasers/as a function of pressure and temperature. Comparisons have been made with calculations based on the AFGL absorption line compilation.

articleTitle: Far Infrared Faraday Rotation Measurement CN ZT-40
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The poloidal magnetic field in ZT-40 (LASL's newest toroidal reversed-field-pinch controlled fusion experiment) is being measured by Faraday rotation of the 164 micron emission of a CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>-pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH laser. The essence of this method, which is independent of spurious intensity modulations, is to monitor the phase distortion of a regular beat frequency. This beating is produced when two oppositely circularly polarized components, frequency shifted with respect to each other and both passed through a magnetized plasma, are transmitted through a linear polarization analyzer. The same concept has been independently described by Dodel and Kunz [1].

articleTitle: Magnetic Resonances (AFMR and SFR) in (CH3NH3)2MnCl4
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: (CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>NH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>)<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>MnCl<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> (abbreviated MAMC) belongs to the family of perovskite-type layer structures the magnetic properties of which show a pronounced quasi-two-dimensional behaviour [1]. In particular, MAMC is a quasi-two-dimensional Heisenberg anti-ferromagnet of the easy axis type [2]. In comparison with the fluoride compounds K<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>MnF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> and Rb<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>MnF<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</inf> within this family [3-5], the chloride compound MAMC with organic molecules has the smallest ani-sotropy field (H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">E</inf> = 81 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup>, H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">A</inf> / H<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">E</inf> ≈ 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−3</sup>). Therefore, the critical field for the spin flop transition is comparatively small.

articleTitle: Experimental Realization of a Distributed Feedback Gas Laser
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The first proposal of a hollow core distributed feedback (DFB) laser was made by Marcuse in 1972 [1]. Since then attempts were made to realize such a laser with optically pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH [2] and with CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> [3] as the active medium. To our knowledge none of these experiments was successfull. The reason was probably insufficient coincidence between the period of the waveguide corrugation and half the wavelength. This coincidence has to be very close since the relative gain bandwidth Δv/v of both active mediums is of the order of 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−4</sup>. This is why successfull operation of DFB was restricted to solid state and dye lasers where the gain bandwidth is much larger.

articleTitle: Design and Fabrication of Improved Hybrid Output Couplers for Optically Pumped Far Infrared Lasers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The behavior of metal mesh dieletric mirrors (MMD) for far infrared applications has been extensively examined by several authors.[1-5] R. Ulrich [1] developed a simple model based on empirical results which are valid in the range 0<g/λ≤.6, where g is the grid constant and λ is the wavelength. His results are based on measurements performed on grids supported by very thin substrates unable to support resonances at the frequencies of interest so that etalon effects due to the substrate do not influence the frequency response of the grids. S. M. Wolfe et al. [2] expanded the analysis of Ulrich and approximated the effects of the substrate on the frequency response of MMD inductive mirrors. It was found that the frequency response of the grids is modified by the etalon effects due to the substrate and that, due to the rapid ocillations in the transmissivity of the mesh mirrors with wavelength, an accurate knowledge of the substrate thickness is necessary for proper design.

articleTitle: A Tunable Sub-Millimeter Laser using Rydberg States of Atomic Potassium
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We report the development of a tunable sub-millimeter laser source, operating in the 100-1000 micrometer wavelength range, using Stark tuned atomic Rydberg states of potassium. The sub-millimeter laser action is generated by optically pumping Rydberg states of atomic potassium vapor with a frequency doubled, etalon tuned, flashlamp pumped dye laser. For example, when the 13p3/2 state is pumped at 292 nanometers, lasing occurs from the 13p to 13s transition (∼116 micrometer) and the 13p to 11d transition (∼78 micrometer). Tuning is accomplished by Stark shifting these energy levels with a small electric (<500 v/cm) field applied to the vapor during optical pumping.

articleTitle: Radiometric Observations of the 752.033-GHz H2O Rotational Absorption Line in Simulated Rocket Plumes
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: A high-resolution (< 1 MHz) two-stage heterodyne receiver has been used to study the 2<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</inf>←2<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">02</inf> rotational absorption line of water vapor both as a thermally broadened ambient and in the flow of a simulated high-altitude rocket plume.

articleTitle: Quantum Limited Millimeter Wave Mixers and Detectors
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We report operation of superconductor-insulator-superconductor quasiparticle tunnel junctions as mixers and detectors at millimeter wavelengths. The voltage scale of the nonlinearity in the I-V curve of such junctions can be small enough that classical device theory breaks down. Calculations based on photon assisted tunneling theory are then necessary to understand the observed performance. The performance predicted in this novel regime is sufficiently good that practical applications appear very promising. The best mixer result observed at 36 GHz is a double side-band mixer noise temperature T<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">m</inf> ≤ 7 K which is about 4 times the photon noise limited value of hv/k. When operated as a direct detector, a current responsivity of 3,500 A/W was observed. This is half the quantum limited value e/hv, which corresponds to one tunneling electron for each incident microwave photon. The best observed NEP was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3 \times 10^{-16}\mathrm{W}\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}</tex>.

articleTitle: Strip-Line Technique in Submillimeter-Magneto Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: In the submillimeter range of radiation the strip-line technique is a useful tool for the investigation of the magneto-optical properties of semiconductors, especially with high carrier concentration. The original form of the strip-line was invented by Drew and Sievers [1] and subsequently repeatedly modified [2, 3, 10]. There are different groups applying successfully this technique for the investigation of highly conductive solids [3-11].

articleTitle: Diagnostic Experiments of the 118 um and 70 um CH3OH Laser Lines
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: We report on a quantitative study of the 118 μm and 70 μm CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH lasers. Quantum theories of FIR lasers have been published [1] [21, but there is not yet quantum model of coupled Doppleror mixed broadened transitions interacting with two intense laser fields and we have followed the fruitful approach of De Temple and Danielewicz [3] in the study of the 496 μm CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F laser. Therefore we have extended the RE model at short FIR wavelengths which requires to introduce the finite velocity width of the population of the upper lasing state created directly by the pump. On the other side the vibrational relaxation to the ground state manifold is synthetized by a single relaxation rate as there are no data available for CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>OH.

articleTitle: Surface Effects in Electron Spin Resonance in Metals with MM Waves
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Conduction electron spin resonance in metals is usually studied in thin plates (thickness ≲ 200 μ) via transmission or in very thin plates (thickness ≲ 20 μ) via reflection. It is therefore not surprising that surface relaxation plays an important role. The dominant spin relaxation mechanism of conduction electrons in the surface is generally thought to be spin-orbit scattering. However, the observed values of ε, the probability that in a collision with the surface there will be a spin reversal, are much higher than those predicted on theoretical grounds. Meservey and Tedrow [1] recently compared values for many metals from different experiments (NMR, Critical fields, spin polarized tunnelling, and electron spin resonance) with a theoretical result obtained by Abrikosov and Gor'kov.

articleTitle: Optically Pumped FIR Laser Monitored by Piezoelectric Transducers
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The power and frequency of a pumped FIR laser can be monitored by piezoelectric transducers, reliable solid state devices which detect chopped absorbed radiation by the opto-acoustic effect.

articleTitle: Assignments of Laser Lines in Optically Pumped CH3CN
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Near-millimeter laser action from optically pumped CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>CN was first obtained by Chang and Mc Gee in 1971 [1]. New emissions were then reported by the same authors [2] and by Radford [3]. At the present the methyl cyanide molecule has been used for obtaining more than thirty lines in the wavelength range from 281 μm up to 1814 μm. Only for the seven lines reported first partial assignments were given. The purpose of this work is to assign more FIR lines through the identification of the rotovibrational transitions of CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>CN which are in coincidence with CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser lines. In similar cases the assignment of the transitions on an optically pumped laser has allowed an analysis of the rotovibrational structure of the active molecule, as in [4] for CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>Br. When for the assigned IR and FIR transitions precise frequency measurements are available, the inclusion of the experimental values in a simultaneously least-squares fit all the spectroscopic data, can provide new accurate sets of molecular constants, as in [5] for CH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>F. Methyl cyanide is a symmetric top molecule, with a large electric dipole moment. Many microwave spectroscopy investigations have been performed and high resolution rotational spectra were recently reported for ground an excited states [6,7]. Extensive studies have been made of the molecular infrared spectrum. The most recent investigations [8, 9] have pointed out the importance of Fermi and Coriolis interactions in the overlapping band systems.

articleTitle: Pressure Broadening and Shifting of Rotation and Rotation-Vibration Spectral Lines of HCL by Noble Gases
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Shifts of the line positions of the 2-0 band of HCl perturbed by noble gases, first measured in 1960 [1,2], were later augmented [3-10] by measurements of linewidths and shifts in the pure rotational and rotation-vibration spectra. To explain the experimental results, several theoretical calculations were performed [11-18] that used primarily the Anderson-Tsao-Curnutte (ATC) theory [19,20]. Whereas qualitative agreement with experiment was obtained, the quantitative agreement was poor.

articleTitle: Metal-Insulator-Metal Point-Contact Diodes
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The paper describes some recent results in understanding and improving metal-insulator-metal point-contact diodes for use as harmonic generators and mixers in laser frequency measurements. The parameters influencing the operation of MIM point-contact diodes are discussed and their implications on thin-film MIM diodes are considered. The theoretical analysis leads to results in good agreement with the experimental data.

articleTitle: Infrared Absorption Spectra of Compensated Single Crystal Silicon using a Fourier Transform Spectrometer
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The infrared absorption spectra of crystalline silicon containing some impurities have been studied in the 200 to 2000 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> region using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) techniques. The excitation spectra associated with the group III acceptor impurities boron and indium and the group V donors, antimony and phosphorus, have been studied at helium temperatures. Fig. 1 shows the schematic and highly simplified energy momentum diagram, and the various electronic transitions due to shallow donors and acceptor (hole transition) centers. Fig. 2 shows the room and 15K spectra of compensated silicon some 0.12 inches thick. The most significant change in the low temperature spectrum is the decrease in absorption and the addition of intense bands in the far infrared region. Fig. 3 shows an expanded plot of two samples at 15K in the 450-150 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> region, in which the P<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3/2</inf> set of transitions for boron are observed. A line seen at 316.1 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−1</sup> is that of phosphorus, which may be compared to previous measurements [1] using grating spectrometers.

articleTitle: A Calibration Source for FIR-Astronomy Experiments
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Requirements: To measure under realistic conditions the responsivity of FIR-detectors as well as the spectral response of Fourier-spectrometers and Fabry-Perot-filters used on balloon-borne telescopes a special calibration source is required.

articleTitle: Finite Element Analysis of Schottky Barrier Diode Structures for Submillimeter Wavelengths
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The numerical technique of finite element analysis has been used to investigate optimum structures for Schottky barrier diodes suitable for submillimeter wavelengths. The effect of different diode shapes, realizable using electron beam lithography, as well as variations in ohmic contact geometry have been studied.

articleTitle: New CW FIR Laser Lines Obtained in Ammonia Pumped by a CO2 Laser, using the Stark Tuning Method
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: It is well known that the ammonia molecule possesses an intense IR absorption spectrum in the 9-10 μm band, corresponding to the wavelengths of the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> laser emission lines [1]. Nevertheless, this situation has not led to numerous Far-Infrared (FIR) laser lines, by CW laser pumping, because of the lack of exact coincidences between the frequencies of the CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> emission lines and those of the absorption transitions of NH<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</inf>. To our knowledge, only two CW FIR lasing lines have so been observed, up to now, using the 9P(17) sequence CO<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> line [2] and two others using the P(13) N<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>O line [3].

articleTitle: Dielectric Relaxation in Some Allyl Compounds
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The possibility of a variety of modes of re-orientation of molecular dipoles, makes the dielectric study of aliphatic molecules interesting [1]. The present paper reports the work aimed at studying the dielectric behaviour of three allyl ethers viz., p-phenyl allyl ether, p-cresyl allyl ether and p-chlorophenyl allyl ether at five frequencies in mm and cm regions at 30°, 50° and 70°C. A new curve fitting technique for evaluating complex permittivity at 4.5 mm for free space method is also described.

articleTitle: Shallow Donors in Transmutation-Doped GaAs in High Magnetic Field
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Germanium and selenium donors have been created in n-GaAs by neutron capture. Line shapes and positions of shallow hydrogenic 1s to 2p (m= −1) donor transitions are studied by Fourier transform spectroscopy and are identified.

articleTitle: Calibration of a Rapid-Scan Polarizing Michelson Interferometer and InSb Detector
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: The application of FIR interferometry to plasma diagnosis requires an accurate relative calibration. Techniques are described whereby calibration using mercury arc lamps and other sources is performed. These calibrations reveal serious channelling problems in the detector and lamp. Modifications in these system elements have been performed to correct these problems.

articleTitle: Circular Polarization of the Spectral Thermal Emission from Mono- and Polycrystalline Iron and Nickel
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Recent spectroscopic investigations of the thermal emission from a single crystal of ferromagnetic iron under the influence of a magnetic field have revealed for the first time a partial circular polarization [1]. This magneto-optic effect has also been verified for polycrystalline samples of iron and nickel. For iron we found identical results for polycrystalline samples and single crystals. Up till now we have not measured single crystals of nickel.

articleTitle: Progress in Submillimeter Antennas
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: There is a need for submillimeter antennas that can be constructed with planar technology. Such antennas are typically more stable than cat-whiskers and lend themselves to integration with devices and to replication in arrays. Early planar submillimeter antennas were long-wire dipoles on the surfaces of thick substrates (1) (2). Such antennas do not have good patterns because they do not guide energy well, tending instead to radiate it quickly into the substrate. One kind of solution to this problem involves reducing radiation into the substrate through use of short antennas, either dipoles (3) or slots (4), and thin substrates. Alternatively one can use a longer antenna and/or thicker substrate by constructing a “sandwich,” i.e. by adding a superstrate so that the antenna is encased in the dielectric (5). Earlier we demonstrated a 118-micron V antenna in a quartz sandwich (6), and the technique has also been used with a long-wire dipole (7).

articleTitle: Fourier Transform Spectroscopy of Electron Cyclotron Radiation from the PLT Tokamak
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Since 1974, there has been a joint research program between the University of Maryland and the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) for studying electron cyclotron emission (ECE) from tokamaks. In 1977, the University of Maryland group began to operate a Fourier transform spectrometer (FTS) on the PLT tokamak at PPPL. The initial results that were obtained with the FTS were reported at the Third International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications in 1978. This paper reports the present state of development of the FTS system on the PLT tokamak and presents examples of the data that has been obtained with it.

articleTitle: Fourth International Conference on Infrared and Millimeter Waves: Editor's Foreword
publicationTitle: 1979 International Conference on Submillimeter Waves and Their Applications
abstract: Ask any conference editor and he'll tell you what a thankless job he has. But secretly he knows he's privileged, because as the papers come in he can survey an entire research field without leaving his desk. This Digest, summarizing the fourth conference in the international infrared-millimeter series, gives the best current survey of our area. The survey becomes especially telling when it is made over the whole conference series. The number of contributed papers has grown remarkably from about 80 at the 1974 Atlanta meeting to about 200 here in Miami. Papers presented this year come from researchers in 16 different countries, carrying on a tradition of broad international coverage started in 1974. The distribution of papers as to research sub-area is noteworthy too. It has changed little since 1974. The largest single area is that of sources, primarily various types of lasers. The second largest area nicely complements the first because it is an application of infrared-millimeter methods; it is solid-state spectroscopy. These two together have accounted for 40 to 55% of each conference's contributed papers. The remaining papers have been spread over about a dozen other identifiable areas with roughly constant percentages but with some significant changes. The 1979 conference shows an increase in papers dealing with infrared-millimeter calibration problems, and a large growth in the area of plasma interactions. The 1980 conference will tell us how the development of these areas continues. The editing of this Digest has been made as easy as possible by the prompt and careful responses of the contributors and it is a pleasure to thank all of you for your efforts.
